title: Moving instead of copying
objectives: Explain move semantics, write a move constructor, and say when a move happens.

screens.title: Which lines copy?
screens.prose: `Tracked` counts its own copies and moves. `make()` returns a `Tracked(1)` by value, `take` takes one by value, and `v` is a reserved `std::vector<Tracked>`. l11 already tapped the copy constructor, so line 2 is familiar. The other lines are new.
screens.question: Tap every line that copies.

hints.text: A named object passed or assigned by value is copied. Which lines do that?
Line 2 is the copy you know. Which other lines hand over a named object that is still needed?
Line 3 casts `a` with `std::move`, so it takes `a` instead of copying it.

feedback.correct: Lines 2, 5 and 8 copy: each passes a named object that stays in use.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A copy happens when a named object that stays alive is passed or assigned by value.

byKey.with-make: You counted the return from `make()` as a copy. Since C++17 a returned temporary is built straight into `d`.
byKey.with-temp: `Tracked(2)` is a temporary, so it is built straight into the parameter. No copy runs.
byKey.with-move: Line 3 moves: it takes the block and writes none of the data.

explain.text: Lines 2, 5 and 8 copy. Lines 3 and 6 move, and lines 4 and 7 build the object in place, so neither runs. A temporary needs no copy because nothing else will use it.

canvas.caption: Lines 2 to 8: copy, move, neither, copy, move, neither, copy.

screens.title: One block, two owners
screens.prose: `a` and `b` are `Buffer`s from l11: a pointer and a size. `a` owns a million doubles. Slide through the three frames and watch where `b` gets its block.
screens.question: How many of the 1,000,000 doubles does the move copy?

widget.accept: None: the move hands the block over

hints.text: Compare the third frame with the second. Is there a second block?

feedback.correct: None. The block did not move; only its owner changed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the doubles written in the third frame.

byKey.all: You counted the copy. A move hands over the block and writes none of the doubles.

explain.text: The copy writes 8,000,000 bytes, about 0.8 ms at 10 GB/s, a round figure. The move writes a pointer and a size: 8 bytes here and 16 on a desktop.

screens.title: What std::move does
screens.prose: An lvalue has a name and an address. An rvalue is a temporary, or a value cast by `std::move`. `Type&&`, met in l11, is a reference that binds to rvalues. `Tracked` counts its copies and moves. After a move the source is **moved-from**: valid and safe to destroy, with a value nobody promises.
screens.question: What does `std::move(a)` do by itself?

options.text: Nothing at run time: it casts `a` to an rvalue reference, so a move can be chosen
It moves the contents of `a` into a temporary
options.why: You read the name literally. The move constructor does the moving; `std::move` only allows it.
`a` is still alive and is destroyed at the end of its scope as usual.

options.text: It sets a flag on `a` that says it may be taken
options.why: There is no flag on the object. The choice is made from the type of the cast.

hints.text: Compare line 2 with line 4. What changed between them?
The first line moved nothing: both counters stay at 0.
The counter moved only on the second line, which has a constructor call.

feedback.correct: It is only a cast. The move constructor does the work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first statement left both counters at zero.

byKey.moves: You read the name literally. The move constructor does the moving; `std::move` only allows it.

explain.text: `std::move(a)` changes how `a` is seen, not what it holds. A move happens only when a constructor or assignment takes that rvalue.

screens.title: Four pushes
screens.prose: Four `v.push_back(Tracked(i))` run on an empty vector. `Tracked`'s move constructor is `noexcept`. This library grows its capacity 1, 2, 4, 8, and the growth factor is a library choice. Growth moves the old elements into the new block.
screens.question: How many copies and how many moves run in all?

hints.text: Each push moves the temporary in. Growth also moves old elements.
The vector grew at the second and third pushes.
Count 4 pushes, 1 element moved at the second push and 2 at the third.

feedback.correct: No copies and 7 moves: 4 for the pushes, 1 and 2 for the two growths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the four pushes, then the old elements moved at each growth.

byKey.r0c1: You may have counted only the four pushes. Growth also moves the old elements: 1 at the second push, 2 at the third.
byKey.r0c0: A vector with a `noexcept` move moves its old elements. It does not copy them.

explain.text: Four moves put the temporaries in. Growth to capacity 2 moved 1 element and growth to 4 moved 2, so 4 + 1 + 2 is 7. The fourth push fits and needs no growth.

screens.title: A move that can throw
screens.prose: Now `Tracked`'s move constructor is not marked `noexcept`. Two pushes of `Tracked(i)` run. This library grows its capacity 1, 2, 4, 8, so the second push grows from 1 to 2.
screens.question: What runs in all?

options.why: You assumed `vector` always moves. It moves only if the move cannot throw; otherwise it copies, so a failure leaves the old block whole.
The pushes still move from the temporaries. Only the relocation copies.
The relocation copies one element, and both pushes move.

hints.text: Two things happen: the pushes, and one relocation at growth.
A temporary can always be moved in.
The relocation copies, because a throwing move would leave the old block half emptied.

feedback.correct: Two moves put the temporaries in, and the growth copies the one old element.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the two pushes from the one relocation.

byKey.all-move: You assumed `vector` always moves. It moves only if the move cannot throw; otherwise it copies.

explain.text: The library calls `std::move_if_noexcept`, which moves only when the move cannot throw (the strong exception guarantee). A move that threw half way would damage the old block, so it copies. A build with exceptions off, such as libc++ with `-fno-exceptions`, moves anyway.

screens.title: Write the moves
screens.prose: This `Buffer` is the l11 class with copy members only, so `std::move(a)` silently copies. Add the two moves. Each takes the block and leaves the source empty, with no allocation.
screens.question: Write `Buffer(Buffer&&) noexcept` and `Buffer& operator=(Buffer&&) noexcept`.

tests.setup: Buffer a(1000, 2.0); reset_alloc_count(); Buffer b = std::move(a);
Buffer a(4, 1.0); Buffer b(2, 9.0); b = std::move(a);
Buffer a(4, 1.0); Buffer b(2, 9.0); b = std::move(a);
Buffer a(1000, 2.0); Buffer b(2, 9.0); reset_alloc_count(); b = std::move(a);
Buffer a(3, 4.0); Buffer& r = a; a = std::move(r);
Buffer a(4, 1.0); Buffer b(2, 9.0); b = std::move(a);
std::vector<Buffer> v; v.reserve(2); v.push_back(Buffer(100, 1.0)); v.push_back(Buffer(100, 2.0)); reset_alloc_count(); v.push_back(Buffer(100, 3.0));
Buffer a(3, 1.0); Buffer b = std::move(a); a = Buffer(2, 7.0);
Buffer a(4, 1.0); Buffer b(2, 9.0); b = std::move(a);

widget.how: Submit runs 15 hidden tests. `alloc_count()` counts calls to `operator new` and `new[]` since the last reset. A move that copies shows as 1 instead of 0. A block never freed fails its test. A moved-from buffer must report size 0 and `data()` null.

hints.text: Copy the two fields across, then reset the source.
The source must end with a null pointer and size 0.
In the assignment, `delete[]` your own block first, and guard with `this != &other`.

feedback.correct: Both moves took the block and left the source empty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing rows. A count above 0 means you allocated. A size above 0 means the source was not emptied.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. Check the `Buffer&&` parameter and the `noexcept` position.

explain.text: A move copies two fields and nulls the source. Nothing allocates, so the cost does not depend on the size.

screens.title: The const that cannot move
screens.prose: `Order` holds a `std::vector<Fill>` of 1,000,000 fills and has the usual special members.
screens.question: What runs for `Order d = std::move(c);`?

options.text: The copy constructor: it copies a million fills

options.why: `std::move` always moves. It yields a `const Order&&`, and the move constructor takes `Order&&`, not const.
It compiles: a `const Order&&` binds to the copy constructor's `const Order&`.
Nothing here is undefined. It is a plain copy of 1,000,000 fills.

hints.text: A move constructor must change its source. Can it change a `const` object?
Which constructors can accept a `const Order`?
Only the copy constructor takes `const Order&`, so overload resolution picks it.

feedback.correct: The copy constructor runs, quietly. The `const` blocked the move.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A move needs to change its source, and `c` is const.

byKey.move: You believed `std::move` always moves. It yields a `const Order&&`, and the move constructor takes `Order&&`.
byKey.error: It compiles: a `const Order&&` binds to the copy constructor's `const Order&`.

explain.text: A move changes the source, and a `const` object cannot be changed. So `std::move(c)` becomes a `const Order&&`, which only the copy constructor accepts. No error, only a million-fill copy.

screens.title: What a moved-from vector holds
screens.prose: After `std::vector<int> w = std::move(v);` the library promises that `v` is valid but in an unspecified state. Your own classes decide for themselves: `Buffer` leaves size 0.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which are always valid on the moved-from `v`?

options.text: `int n = v.size();` (valid, but the value is unspecified)

options.why: A moved-from vector may be empty. Nothing promises an element at index 0.
`back()` needs a non-empty vector, and a moved-from one may be empty.

hints.text: Which operations need the vector to hold something?
Destroying, assigning, clearing and asking the size work on any valid vector, empty or not.
Indexing and `back()` need an element to exist.

feedback.correct: Destroy, assign, clear and `size()` need nothing in the vector.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the operations that work on an empty vector.

explain.text: A moved-from object is valid, so any call with no precondition on its contents is safe. That includes `size()`, though its result is unspecified. Reading an element needs a size, and the library promises none.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.question: What must a move constructor leave behind in the source?

options.text: A valid object that is safe to destroy
The source unchanged, so it can be used again
options.why: Then both objects own the block and it is freed twice.

options.text: Nothing: the source is already deleted
options.why: The source is destroyed later, so its destructor must still be safe.

feedback.correct: The source must be valid and safe to destroy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The source still gets destroyed at the end of its scope.

explain.text: Nulling the pointer makes the source destructor a harmless `delete[] nullptr`. That is why the move assignment tests `this != &o` before freeing its own block.

screens.title: A setter that keeps its argument
screens.question: How many doubles does each call copy?

hints.text: The parameter is built first. Then the assignment moves from it.
A named lvalue is copied into the parameter; a moved or returned value is not.
The assignment into the member is always a move.

feedback.correct: Only the first call copies, once, into the parameter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask for each call how the parameter is built.

byKey.r0c1: You counted two copies. The parameter is the copy; the assignment into the member is a move.
byKey.r1c1: You counted a copy for `std::move(history)`. The parameter takes its block, and nothing is copied.
byKey.r2c1: `load()` returns a temporary, so it is built straight into the parameter. The assignment then moves it.

explain.text: The copy is made once, where the caller passes a named lvalue. Everywhere else the parameter takes a block that was already going. Interviewers call this a sink argument.

ideas: A copy duplicates what an object owns. A move takes it from an object that is about to go, and leaves it empty and safe to destroy.
`std::move` is only a cast to an rvalue reference. The move constructor does the moving, and a `const` object cannot be moved, so it copies.
A vector moves its old elements on growth only if their move is `noexcept`. Otherwise it copies, to keep the old block whole.

formula.name: The move pattern
formula.note: Take the pointer, null the source, mark it noexcept.

summary.trap: Writing `return std::move(t);` blocks elision, so a move runs where `return t;` would run none.

options.text: It casts `a` to an rvalue reference and moves nothing itself
It moves the contents of `a` into a new object
options.why: The move constructor does that. `std::move` only makes a move possible.
`a` stays alive and is destroyed at the end of its scope.
It makes `a` look like a temporary, which is the opposite of const.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the cast changes.

explain.text: `std::move` changes how `a` is seen. A constructor or assignment that takes `T&&` then does the move.

quiz.question: How many of the three calls copy?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which arguments are named objects that stay alive.

byKey.three: You counted every call. Only a named object passed as it is must be copied.

explain.text: The named `a` is copied. `std::move(a)` moves, and `Tracked(3)` is built straight into the parameter.

quiz.prose: A `std::vector<T>` must grow, and `T`'s move constructor is not `noexcept`.
quiz.question: Why does it copy the old elements?

options.text: A throw half way through moving would leave the old block damaged; copying keeps it whole
Copying is faster than moving for small objects
options.why: Moving is never slower. The reason is safety when a move can throw.

options.text: The vector cannot call a move that might throw
options.why: It can call it. It chooses not to when a copy is available.

options.text: A move would leave the new elements empty
options.why: A move fills the new elements. The risk is a throw part way.

feedback.correct: Safety wins: the copy keeps the old block whole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what a throw does half way through.

explain.text: The library calls `std::move_if_noexcept`. A copy that throws leaves the old block intact, a move that throws does not.

quiz.question: Which constructor runs for `d`?

options.why: It takes `Order&&`, and a `const Order&&` does not bind to that.
It compiles. The `const Order&&` binds to the copy constructor.
Elision applies to a returned temporary, not to a `std::move` of a named object.

feedback.correct: A const object can only be copied.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The move constructor needs a non-const source.

explain.text: Moving changes the source, so a const source falls back to the copy constructor.

quiz.question: What does the `std::move` do here?

options.text: It blocks copy elision, so a move runs where plain `return t;` would run none

options.why: A returned local is already treated as an rvalue, and elision builds it in place for free.

options.text: It is needed, or the compiler would copy
options.why: The compiler moves a returned local without being asked.
It changes what runs: a move replaces the elision.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the counts of the two spellings.

explain.text: On the desk compiler `return t;` ran 0 moves and `return std::move(t);` ran 1. Let the compiler move for you.
